item: The low-carbon option as the default
example: "Your plan is renewable power at the same price. Switch any time."
effect: Green share of contracts up {ebeling} points; plant-based share of meals up {food_lo} to {food_hi} points
fails: It changes the choice at one counter or form, not what people eat all day. The effect is weaker when the price or the effort to opt out rises.
cite: Ebeling and Lotz 2015; Boronowsky et al. 2022

item: More low-carbon dishes, the others kept
example: "Half the main dishes are plant-based, and the burger is still there."
effect: Vegetarian share of meals sold up {menu_lo} to {menu_hi} points
fails: It works only where the dishes are good and are served. In 18 worksites that made part of the change, the share moved 2.3 points; one analysis found this significant and the other did not.
cite: Garnett et al. 2019; Arrazat et al. 2024; Pechey et al. 2022

item: A dish named for its taste, not for what it lacks
effect: 14 percent more diners took vegetables than with plain names, 29 percent more than with health names
evidence: Preregistered field study, 137,842 diner decisions, 5 US dining halls
fails: The study tested vegetables, not meat swaps. There was no effect at the dining hall with the least tasty food.

item: An ask for less, not none
example: "Could we skip meat two days a week?"
effect: 6.9 points more meatless meals than a go-vegetarian appeal, not significant. 59 percent took a reduction pledge, against 15 percent for a vegetarian pledge
evidence: Preregistered field trial, 617 students, one university cafe
fails: Neither appeal beat no appeal. Of those who took the reduction pledge, 32 percent then chose a meatless meal, against 48 percent of vegetarian pledgers.

item: The honest size of a small step
example: "Green power is a good step. It covers a small part of household emissions; most come from other sources."
effect: Where a green default lowered support for a carbon tax from 70 to 60 percent, one sentence on the default's small effect raised it to 72 percent
fails: Hypothetical votes, one research group. No study has measured real policy outcomes.

item: What most people already think and do
example: "Most people here want more renewable power."
effect: Donations to a climate charity rose 12 dollars, 4.7 percent, when people learned that 62 percent of Americans try to fight global warming
evidence: Online experiment with real money, United States
fails: One study, measured immediately. A norm below what the audience already does can pull them down.
cite: Andre et al. 2026; Schultz et al. 2007

item: A messenger who already does it
example: "We put panels on last spring. Come and see the bill."
effect: Volunteers who had solar panels themselves recruited 62.8 percent more installations
fails: One program. An activist image or a superior tone lowers willingness.

example: "Using less power means less pollution from power plants, which is linked to childhood asthma."
effect: Health and environment messages cut electricity use 8.2 percent; cost messages saved nothing measurable
fails: One building complex. Real money still moves large purchases.

item: A named threat paired with one step
example: "The heat waves are getting worse. The boiler is the largest thing this house controls, and a grant pays half."
effect: Fear appeals worked better with a step attached (d 0.43 against 0.21); in the 63-country test, no message raised effort on the tree-planting task
fails: In the tournament, the negative-emotion message raised sharing and lowered effort.
cite: Tannenbaum et al. 2015; Vlasceanu et al. 2024

example: "One vetted installer, one price for the whole town, a free site visit."
effect: 37 more solar installations per campaign town; free home retrofits went from under 1 to about 6 percent take-up
evidence: Field programs and trials, Connecticut and Michigan
fails: The campaign effect stopped when the campaign did. Outreach cost more than 1,000 dollars per extra home.
cite: Gillingham and Bollinger 2021; Fowlie, Greenstone and Wolfram 2018

item: Upfront cost and paperwork cut, not facts added
example: "Nothing to pay upfront, and the grant forms are done for you."
effect: Efficiency information alone did not change water-heater purchases; a 100-dollar rebate did
evidence: Field trial, US retail call center
fails: Rebates cost money per tonne. Stated-choice surveys overstate uptake.

item: Comparison with similar neighbors, plus approval
example: "You used 12 percent less than similar homes nearby." with a smiley
effect: Home energy reports cut electricity use 1.3 to 2.0 percent
evidence: Field trials, millions of US homes
fails: Small, and smaller at scale. Below-average users shown the average raised their use, unless the report added approval.

item: Use shown where and when it happens
example: A shower display that counts liters as the water runs
effect: Shower energy fell 22 percent at home, 11.4 percent in hotels
fails: The repeat with hotel guests gave half the effect.
cite: Tiefenbeck et al. 2018; Tiefenbeck et al. 2019
